Text: When assessing an older patient, do not limit your assessment to the {{c1::obvious problem}}.
Back Extra:
Why: you are there to listen and act on everything you learn, not only to treat the complaint that first stands out.

Cue: think of the patient as someone's grandmother or grandfather, or as yourself when you reach that age.
coverage_notes: Don't-limit-assessment rule; folds U-M3's praised empathy anchor as the Cue line.

Text: Older patients who say they feel unwell, or who seem overly concerned about their health, are at risk for a serious {{c1::decline}} in their physical, emotional, or psychological state.
Back Extra:
Pitfall: do not dismiss an older patient's vague complaint or excessive worry as exaggeration, since such concern may warn of a serious decline.

Cue: the decline may be physical, emotional, or psychological, so stay alert to all three.
coverage_notes: Second must-test of U-M1: voiced unwellness signals decline risk.

Text: You must never attribute a patient's altered mental status to {{c1::old age}}.
Back Extra:
Why: altered mental status has treatable causes that must be found, not dismissed.

Pitfall: dismissing new confusion as normal aging can miss a dangerous but reversible problem.
coverage_notes: The NEVER rule as a negation card.

Text:
Hostility, irritability, or confusion in an older patient may be caused by six problems:
{{c1::hypoxia (lack of oxygen)}}
{{c1::brain injury, including stroke}}
{{c1::unintentional drug overdose}}
{{c1::infection}}
{{c1::abnormal blood glucose level}}
{{c1::insufficient perfusion}}
Back Extra:
Meaning: perfusion is the circulation of blood, and therefore nutrients, to the cells.

Why: each cause is treatable, so finding the reason for an older patient's confusion can be lifesaving.
coverage_notes: Cohesive 6-cause grouped list; perfusion prerequisite closed via the source's parenthetical.

Text: A previously sharp 85-year-old suddenly becomes confused and irritable, and his family says he is "just getting old." Rather than accepting that explanation, you should {{c1::assess for treatable medical causes::next action}}.
Back Extra:
Pitfall: new confusion in an older patient is a treatable emergency until proven otherwise, never simply "old age."

Cue: a family's "he's just getting old" is a reason to assess harder, not to relax.
coverage_notes: Auto-paired vignette. Consolidation rewrite: original answer (an underlying medical problem) failed the one-answer test; now tests the next ACTION, which no sibling spells out verbatim.

Text: An older patient with a chronic disease such as diabetes may report {{c1::no pain}} even after a fall or injury.
Back Extra:
Why: chronic disease can blunt pain perception, and older patients may not be fully aware of important changes in their body systems.

Pitfall: absence of pain does not rule out injury, so watch closely for objective changes, however subtle.
coverage_notes: Recall half of the auto-pair.

Text: An 82-year-old diabetic fell an hour ago but reports no pain. Because pain can be masked, stay especially vigilant for subtle {{c1::objective changes::what to watch for}} in her condition.
Back Extra:
Why: chronic disease such as diabetes can blunt pain, so a diabetic patient may not feel or report an injury.

Pitfall: never let a normal or absent pain report convince you a patient is uninjured.
coverage_notes: Vignette half of the auto-pair; tests the countermeasure with the source's exact term.

Text:
Before an older patient leaves for the hospital, help locate three personal items that will significantly improve their stay:
{{c1::hearing aids}}
{{c1::eyeglasses}}
{{c1::dentures}}
Back Extra:
Why: hearing aids, eyeglasses, and dentures let the patient hear, see, and eat, which can greatly improve a hospital stay.

Cue: if appropriate, also help the patient pack a few other personal items before leaving.
coverage_notes: Cohesive 3-item grouped list; extractor PARTIAL was a layout artifact, verified on the page 376 render.

Text: One of the most effective ways to calm a frightened child is to first calm the child's {{c1::parent or caregiver}}.
Back Extra:
Why: children take cues from their parents or caregivers, so a calm adult reassures and calms the child in turn.

Cue: be honest with children as well, since they easily see through lies or deception.
coverage_notes: Calm-the-caregiver fact; mechanism in Back Extra to avoid decoding.

Text: If a hard-of-hearing patient's hearing aid is missing after a fall or illness, find it in two ways: {{c1::look in the immediate area}}, or {{c1::ask the patient or family}}.
Back Extra:
Pitfall: a hearing aid is easily lost in a fall or forgotten when the patient is confused or ill, so check early.

Cue: most hard-of-hearing patients have normal intelligence and can read lips, so face them and let them see your lips.
coverage_notes: Two locate-methods grouped under one cloze.

Text:
Five steps to communicate with a patient who is hard of hearing:
1. {{c1::keep paper and a pen ready to write questions and answers}}
2. {{c1::face the patient and speak distinctly at a normal pace}}
3. {{c1::never shout}}
4. {{c1::listen carefully; ask short questions and give short answers}}
5. {{c1::learn simple sign-language phrases}}
Back Extra:
Why: shouting does not help the patient hear and may frighten them.

Cue: the three most useful signs to learn are 'sick,' 'hurt,' and 'help.'

Pitfall: do not cover your mouth or mumble, since most hard-of-hearing patients read lips.
coverage_notes: Cohesive ordered 5-step list in one grouped card; count verified against the full source list.

Text:
Managing a patient who has a guide dog:
Patient stable → {{c1::transport the dog with the patient::Stable}}
Patient unstable, dog injured or unruly, or another safety concern → {{c1::arrange separate care for the dog::Unstable}}
Back Extra:
Why: transporting the dog with a stable patient reduces stress for both the patient and the dog.

Cue: a guide dog wears a special harness and is trained not to leave its master or respond to strangers.

Pitfall: when the dog cannot ride along, contact your supervisor and follow local protocol.
coverage_notes: Branch card with role-label hints; both arms present.

Text: When taking a history from a patient who speaks little English, help them understand by {{c1::pointing to specific body parts}} as you ask your questions.
Back Extra:
Pitfall: speaking louder does not increase a patient's ability to understand you.

Cue: first find out how much English the patient speaks, then use short, simple questions and avoid medical terms.
coverage_notes: Highlighted technique; louder-does-not-help gold as the Pitfall.

Text: In mission-critical communications, a {{c1::mental model}} is {{c2::the picture in a person's head of "what's going on"}}.
Back Extra:
Distinguish: a mental model is the picture itself; situational awareness is what fails when teammates' pictures stop matching.

Why: team members in different roles see different things from different perspectives, so effective teamwork requires all members to share one mental model.
coverage_notes: Two-way definition of mental model.

Text: {{c1::Mission-critical communications}} are any communications where {{c2::disruption will result in failure of the task at hand}}.
Back Extra:
Cue: the concept central to mission-critical communications is the shared mental model.

Ex: a patient care handover — disrupt it and the task it serves (continuing the patient's care) fails.
coverage_notes: Two-way definition; central-concept framing in the Cue line.

Text: The goal of mission-critical communications is an efficient, effective, and error-free {{c1::transfer}} of the {{c1::mental model}}.
Back Extra:
Why: success means the receiver ends up seeing "what's going on" the same way the sender does — moving words alone is not the goal.

Cue: the three goal descriptors all start with e — efficient, effective, error-free.
coverage_notes: GOAL fact; load-bearing pair clozed.

Text: When team members' mental models differ — different pictures of "what's going on" — {{c1::situational awareness}} fails and problems begin.
Back Extra: Why: providers in different roles see different things from different perspectives, so a shared mental model has to be deliberately built.
coverage_notes: Failure-mode fact.

Text:
To build a mental model of a patient, a provider or team must answer four questions in sequence:
1. {{c1::What is the focused priority for the patient?}}
2. {{c1::What is the history of prior care?}}
3. {{c1::What is the patient's current state?}}
4. {{c1::What are the patient's immediate needs?}}
Back Extra:
Cue: crux of the problem → what got us to this point → where we are right now → the very next thing that needs to happen.

Why: answering all four quickly and efficiently lets receiving clinicians continue forward progress instead of spending time on unnecessary questions.
coverage_notes: Ordered grouped 4-question list; glosses moved to the Cue line.

Text: {{c1::Patient care handover}} is the transfer of {{c2::pertinent patient information}} and {{c2::responsibility for the patient's care}}.
Back Extra: Ex: handover often involves the physical movement of the patient and associated equipment.
coverage_notes: Two-way definition; both meaning components share c2.

Text:
Giving a handover report follows a five-point method, in order:
1. {{c1::Initiate eye contact}}
2. {{c1::Manage the environment}}
3. {{c1::Ensure the ABCs}}
4. {{c1::Provide a structured report}}
5. {{c1::Provide documentation}}
Back Extra:
Why: eye contact marks that the handover is beginning and identifies who is reporting and who is receiving — "We are communicating now, you and I."

Pitfall: avoid moving the patient during the report — movement pulls both parties' attention away from the patient information.

Distinguish: the RECEIVING method swaps in maintain eye contact, ensure understanding, summarize, and gather documentation — the five-point frame works in virtually all handover situations.
coverage_notes: Rule 0 synthesis: six adjacent highlights become ONE grouped ordered card.

Text: You arrive at the ED with CPR in progress on your patient. The needed critical care is conveyed and addressed {{c1::immediately::immediately or after the report}}, and the full handover report may be {{c1::delayed::delayed or given as usual}}.
Back Extra:
Why: priority critical care that must be initiated or continued comes first — the full report waits until the immediate life threat is addressed.

Ex: an endotracheal tube that must be placed on arrival gets addressed by the receiving clinician before the full report.

Cue: "Ensure the ABCs" is point 3 of the five-point giving method.
coverage_notes: Sibling application card for the Ensure-the-ABCs delay nuance.

Text: A handover's verbal report should carry {{c1::only the immediately critical information}}, with the numerous other details transferring via {{c1::a paper or electronic report}}.
Back Extra:
Cue: the verbal content is exactly the four mental-model answers — priority conditions, prior care, current state, and immediate needs.

Why: the receiving team must grasp the priorities now; the numerous remaining details stay retrievable in the documentation.
coverage_notes: Provide-documentation split card.

Text:
The structured handover format SBAR stands for:
{{c1::Situation::S}}
{{c1::Background::B}}
{{c1::Assessment::A}}
{{c1::Recap/Rx::R}}
Back Extra:
Meaning: S = a concise statement of the problem; B = relevant, brief background on the patient situation; A = your assessment findings and what you think.

Why: research on mission-critical communications shows a structured format greatly improves efficiency and reduces errors; SBAR is not inherently superior to other formats but is widely used and well understood in hospitals.

Distinguish: EMS sometimes modifies SBAR to SBAT, where Treatment replaces Recap/Rx.
coverage_notes: Acronym grouped card with first-letter hints; also grounds the structured-format research rationale (giving point 4).

Text: In the EMS-modified version of SBAR ({{c1::SBAT::acronym}}), the final component becomes {{c1::Treatment::T}} rather than recap/Rx.
Back Extra:
Meaning: T = Treatment — the care that has been provided to the patient.

Cue: S, B, and A keep their SBAR meanings; only the final letter changes for EMS.
coverage_notes: SBAT variant card clozing only the changed element.

Text:
Receiving a handover report follows a five-point method, in order:
1. {{c1::Maintain eye contact}}
2. {{c1::Manage the environment}}
3. {{c1::Ensure understanding}}
4. {{c1::Summarize}}
5. {{c1::Gather supplementary patient documentation}}
Back Extra:
Distinguish: the giver INITIATES eye contact to open the exchange; the receiver MAINTAINS it.

Ex: many hospitals set a moment of silence during trauma, cardiac, stroke, sepsis, and other alerts; in the field, at least pause during the report to focus on key information.

Why: "Ensure understanding" means asking questions as necessary to clarify and correct any issues once the report is received.
coverage_notes: Rule 0 synthesis: six adjacent highlights become ONE grouped ordered card.

Text: When receiving a handover, the "Summarize" step is not a repeat of the entire report — it is a spoken summary of the receiver's {{c1::mental model::2 words}}.
Back Extra:
Why: stating the summary aloud lets the reporting provider and receiving team ask questions or correct errors, ensuring the shared mental model is correct.

Cue: Summarize is point 4 of the five-point receiving method.
coverage_notes: Summarize-nuance sibling card.

Text: A {{c1::patient care report (PCR)}} is the {{c2::legal::legal/medical/administrative}} document used to record all aspects of the care a patient received, from {{c3::initial dispatch}} to {{c3::arrival at the hospital}}.
Back Extra:
Meaning: PCR is also called the prehospital care report — either term is acceptable.

Cue: usually completed after care is transferred to ED staff; finishing en route works only when the trip is long and the patient needs minimal care.
coverage_notes: Three-direction definition note: name, legal nature, dispatch-to-arrival span.

Text: The two types of patient care reports are {{c1::written}} and {{c1::electronic (ePCRs)}}.
Back Extra:
Meaning: ePCR = electronic patient care report.

Cue: whichever type is used, the PCR remains the legal record of the call.
coverage_notes: Small grouped fact.

Text: The documentation adage warns: "If the report looks sloppy, the {{c1::patient care}} was also sloppy."
Back Extra:
Why: a PCR projects a professional or nonprofessional image — readers treat the report's appearance as a proxy for the quality of the care behind it.

Cue: neat, concise, well written, with correct spelling and grammar — the look that reflects good patient care.
coverage_notes: Adage as the memorable hook with the payoff clozed.

Text: Standard procedure in EMS documentation is to record times in {{c1::military (24-hour)}} time, where every recorded time is {{c2::unique}}.
Back Extra: Ex: 1:00 PM is written as 1300; 12 noon cannot be confused with 12 midnight.
coverage_notes: Concept card only; flagged for the numeric worked example (1300) and the noon/midnight facts.

Text: The {{c1::narrative::PCR section}} is arguably the {{c2::most important}} portion of the patient care report — the place to describe all the facts related to the EMS call.
Back Extra: Cue: the narrative tells the story of the call — findings, actions, and the effect on the patient.
coverage_notes: Section name + most-important status.

Text: A PCR narrative should tell the story and present a clear, detailed picture of three things: {{c1::what you found}}, {{c1::what you did}}, and {{c1::how it affected the patient's condition}}.
Back Extra:
Cue: found → did → effect — assessment findings, interventions given, and the patient's response.

Why: a reader should be able to rebuild the call's story from findings, actions, and effect alone.
coverage_notes: Cohesive grouped triple; PARTIAL grounding was a layout artifact, verified on the page 399-400 renders.
